turnos.texto: The Hare and the Tortoise. In the forest lived a very fast hare who was always bragging:
Nobody runs like me!
One day, a tortoise calmly said to her:
I challenge you to a race.
All the animals laughed, but the race began. The hare shot off like lightning and soon left the tortoise far behind.
I have plenty of time,

she thought, and lay down to sleep under a tree. Meanwhile, the tortoise walked step by step, never stopping. She passed the sleeping hare and kept going. When the hare woke up, she ran with all her strength, but it was too late: the tortoise was crossing the finish line. Everyone cheered for the tortoise, who smiled happily. Moral: Little by little, without giving up, you get further than by running and bragging.
The Lion and the Mouse. A lion was sleeping in the sun when a little mouse, playing, ran right over his nose. The lion woke up angry and caught him with his enormous paw.
Please, let me go!
begged the mouse.
Someday I will help you.
The lion roared with laughter:
You, so small, help me?

But he let him go. Days later, some hunters caught the lion in a net. The lion roared and roared, but he could not get out. The little mouse heard the roars and came running. With his small, sharp teeth he chewed the rope, again and again, until the net broke. The lion was free and said:
Thank you, friend. Now I know that little ones can help a lot too.
Moral: Nobody is too small to help. Do good, and good comes back to you.
The Grasshopper and the Ant. All summer long, the grasshopper sang and played her guitar under the trees. The ant, instead, spent her days carrying grains of wheat to her home.
Why do you work so hard?
teased the grasshopper.
Come and sing with me.
I am saving food for the winter,
answered the ant. Winter came with its cold and its snow. The grasshopper had nothing to eat, and shivering, she knocked on the ant’s door. The ant let her in and shared her food with her.
Thank you,
said the grasshopper, embarrassed.
Next summer I will sing, but I will also save for when I need it.
Moral: There is time to play and time to work: whoever saves today will have tomorrow.
The Boy Who Cried Wolf. A shepherd boy looked after his sheep on the hill. One day, bored, he shouted:
Help, the wolf is coming!
The people of the village ran up to help him, but there was no wolf. The boy laughed and laughed. Days later he shouted again:
The wolf, the wolf!
Once again the people ran up the hill, and once again it was a lie. One afternoon, the wolf really came.
Help, the wolf is here!

shouted the boy with all his might. But this time nobody came, because nobody believed him. The wolf scared the sheep and took them away. The boy, very sad, learned that when you lie, later nobody believes you even when you tell the truth. Moral: Always tell the truth: trust is hard to earn and easy to lose.
The Fox and the Grapes. A very hungry fox was walking through the field when she saw some purple grapes hanging from a very tall vine.
They look so tasty!

she thought. She jumped to reach them, but she couldn’t. She jumped again, higher, and still couldn’t. She tried many times until she was tired and out of breath. Then she lifted her nose, turned around and said:
Bah, I don’t even want them. I’m sure they are green and sour.
A little bird who saw her from a branch said:
They are not green, friend fox. You just couldn’t reach them.
The fox walked away, a little ashamed. Moral: When we can’t do something, it is better to accept it or try another way than to say we didn’t want it.

The Crow and the Pitcher. It was a very hot day and a crow was very thirsty. He flew and flew until he found a pitcher with a little bit of water at the bottom. He put his beak in, but he couldn’t reach the water. He tried to knock the pitcher over, but it was too heavy. The crow stopped to think. Then he had an idea: he picked up a pebble with his beak and dropped it into the pitcher. Then another, and another one. With each pebble, the water rose a little bit. After many pebbles, the water reached the top. The crow drank happily until he was no longer thirsty. By thinking calmly, he had found the solution. Moral: When something seems impossible, think calmly: intelligence and patience often find the way.

The Hen That Laid the Golden Eggs. A farmer and his wife had a very special hen: every morning she laid a golden egg. With each egg they bought what they needed and lived peacefully. But one day the farmer thought:
If the hen lays golden eggs, inside she must be full of gold. That way we’ll be rich all at once!
His wife said:
Wait, let’s keep things as they are,

but he did not listen. Without thinking any more, he opened the hen to look for the treasure. Inside there was no gold at all: she was a hen like any other. And from that day on, there were no more golden eggs. The farmer understood, too late, that by wanting everything at once he lost everything. Moral: Whoever wants it all loses it all. Take care of what you have and be thankful.

The Fox and the Stork. A playful fox invited the stork to eat. She served her a very tasty soup, but on a flat plate. The fox lapped it up, while the stork, with her long beak, couldn’t taste a single drop.
Didn’t you like it?

asked the fox, laughing. The stork said nothing and, when saying goodbye, invited the fox to eat the next day. When the fox arrived, the stork served the food in tall, thin jars. The stork ate happily, putting in her long beak, but the fox couldn’t fit her snout inside. The fox went home hungry, thinking:
Now I know how she felt.
Since then, when she invites someone, she first thinks about what her guest needs. Moral: Treat others the way you would like to be treated.
The Two Friends and the Bear. Two friends were walking together through the forest.
No matter what happens, we will take care of each other,

they promised. Suddenly, an enormous bear appeared. One of the friends, without thinking of the other, quickly climbed a tree and hid among the branches. The other friend couldn’t climb in time. He lay down on the ground and stayed very still, without breathing. The bear came close, sniffed him... and, since he didn’t move, went back the way he came. The friend in the tree came down and asked, nervously:
What did the bear whisper in your ear?
The other answered:
He told me not to walk with friends who leave me alone when there is danger.
Moral: You find out who your true friends are in difficult times.
The Wind and the Sun. One day, the wind and the sun were arguing about who was the strongest.
Let’s see who can make that man take off his coat,

said the sun. The wind went first. It blew and blew with tremendous strength. But the harder it blew, the tighter the man held on to his coat so he wouldn’t be cold. Tired, the wind gave up. Then the sun came out from behind the clouds and shone soft and warm. The man felt the warmth, wiped his forehead and, very comfortable, took off his coat all by himself. The wind understood that the sun had won without shouting and without pushing, just with its warmth. Moral: Kindness achieves more than force.

The Posada on Luna Street. On Luna Street, all the neighbors got together every December to hold the posada. That year it was Lupita’s family’s turn. In the afternoon, the children were given little candles and paper lanterns. They walked slowly, singing, from house to house, asking for shelter, as Joseph and Mary did long ago. At the last house, the door opened and everyone shouted with joy:
Come in, pilgrims!
Inside there was warm ponche, tamales and an enormous piñata. Lupita saw that Don Ramón, the neighbor on the corner, was watching from his window.
Mom, can we invite him?
she asked. Don Ramón came over smiling.
It has been years since anyone invited me,
he said. That night, the posada was happier than ever. Something to think about: Christmas is more fun when nobody is left out.
The Seven-Pointed Piñata. Mateo and his grandpa made a star piñata with seven points. They used a clay pot, newspaper, homemade glue and lots of colored paper.
Why does it have seven points, Grandpa?
asked Mateo. His grandpa explained:
They say each point is something we want to take out of our lives, like anger, laziness or selfishness. When we break the piñata, good things come out.
At the posada, Mateo put on the blindfold. Everyone sang:
Hit it, hit it, hit it!

He swung once, twice... and the piñata broke! Out fell peanuts, tangerines, sugar cane and candy. Mateo filled his hands, but he saw his little cousin with nothing. Without thinking, he gave her half. His grandpa winked at him: the selfishness was already gone. Something to think about: What you share is worth more than what you keep only for yourself.

The Little Lamb of the Nativity. Every year, Sofía helped her grandma set up the nativity scene. They took out of a box Mary, Joseph, the little donkey, the ox, the shepherds and the little lambs. But this time one little lamb was missing. They searched the whole box and it didn’t turn up. Sofía felt sad:
The nativity won’t be complete.
Grandma took out a bit of clay and said:
Let’s make a new one.

With her fingers, Sofía shaped it: a round body, little ears and four little legs. She let it dry and painted it white. It wasn’t perfect: one ear was bigger than the other. But when she placed it next to the shepherds, Grandma said:
It is the most special little lamb, because you made it.
And ever since, every December, Sofía looks for it first. Something to think about: What we make with our hands and with love has a special value.

The Poinsettia Flower. A long time ago, in a town in Mexico, there lived a girl named Pepita. On Christmas Eve, everyone brought a gift to baby Jesus at the town church. Pepita was very poor and had nothing to bring. She was walking sadly when she saw some green branches beside the road.
It’s just a little, but I give it with all my heart,
she thought, and she picked them. Some children laughed at her:
Those are just weeds!

Pepita said nothing. She went into the church and lovingly placed her branches. Then something wonderful happened: the top leaves turned a bright red, like stars. Since that day, that flower is called Nochebuena, and it decorates homes every December. The ancient Mexicans knew it as cuetlaxóchitl. Something to think about: What matters about a gift is the love it is given with, not its price.

Christmas Eve Tamales. On December 24th, the kitchen at Emiliano’s house filled with people. The whole family was going to make tamales for Christmas Eve dinner. Grandma prepared the dough. Dad soaked the corn husks. Mom cooked the chicken filling with green salsa, and Aunt Rosa made the sweet pink ones.
And what do I do?
asked Emiliano.
You are going to spread the dough on the husks,
said Grandma. At first they came out crooked, but little by little they turned out better and better. That night, when the pot let out its delicious steam, everyone sat down at the table.
These tamales taste better because we all made them together,
said Grandma. And Emiliano smiled, with his face covered in dough. Something to think about: When everyone helps, work becomes a party.
Don Chuy’s Ponche. Don Chuy sold corn on the cob on the corner, but every December he swapped his cart for a big pot of ponche. The neighborhood children couldn’t wait for him.
What do you put in your ponche, Don Chuy?
asked Camila. He showed her:
Guava, tejocote, sugar cane, apple, prunes, cinnamon and piloncillo. And most important of all: patience, so it simmers slowly.
One very cold day, Camila saw that some men sweeping the street had frozen hands. She said to Don Chuy:
What if we give them some ponche?

Don Chuy smiled and filled several cups. The men warmed their hands with the cups and said thank you. That afternoon, Camila learned that ponche warms your tummy, but sharing it warms your heart. Something to think about: A small act of kindness can warm someone’s day.
The Star That Came Late. In the sky lived a very small little star who was always late for everything. The big stars made fun of her:
You are so tiny that nobody can see you!

On Christmas night, all the stars took their places to shine over the world. The little star, as always, fell asleep and arrived last. While she was looking for her place, she saw a boy lost in the countryside, crying, unable to find the way home. Nobody else had seen him. The little star came down a bit and shone with all her might. The boy followed her light until he reached his town, where his family hugged him. From that night on, the big stars stopped making fun of her. They learned that no light is so small that it can’t guide someone. Something to think about: No matter how small you are: you can always help someone.

Valeria’s Letter to the Three Kings. On January 5th, Valeria sat down to write her letter to the Three Kings: Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar. She really wanted to ask for a bicycle. But she remembered her little brother Tomás, who always played with a broken ball. And her grandma, who was cold in the mornings. Valeria thought for a while, erased the bicycle and wrote something else.
Dear Three Kings: this year I want to ask you for a new ball for Tomás and a warm blanket for my grandma. If you have anything left, a box of crayons for me. With love, Valeria.
She left the letter in her shoe by the window. The next morning, there was a ball, a blanket... and a box of crayons with a little note:
Thank you for thinking of others. Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
Something to think about: Thinking of others fills us with joy too.

The Little Doll in the Rosca. On January 6th, Diego’s family got together to cut the rosca de Reyes. It was big and round, with colorful fruit paste and sugar on top, and a cup of hot chocolate for everyone.
Inside the rosca there is a little hidden doll,
explained Mom.
Whoever finds it will have to treat everyone to tamales on February 2nd, Candelaria Day.
Everyone cut their piece carefully. Uncle Beto found nothing. Grandma didn’t either. Diego bit into his bread and... there was the little doll! Everyone clapped and shouted:
Diego is buying the tamales!
Diego got worried:
But I don’t know how to make tamales.
Grandma hugged him:
Don’t worry, we’ll make them together, like on Christmas Eve.
And so, the party already had a date to get together again. Something to think about: Traditions are a reason to be together again.
Sofía’s Twelve Grapes. On December 31st, Sofía’s family made New Year’s dinner. Before midnight, Mom gave everyone a little plate with twelve grapes.
With each chime of the clock, you eat a grape and make a wish,
she explained.
There are twelve, one for each month of the year that is starting.

Sofía thought about her wishes very carefully: learning to ride a bike, her dog Canelo getting better, getting good grades, reading more stories... and more. When the clock began to chime, she ate the grapes so fast that she almost choked, and everyone laughed. After the last chime, everyone hugged:
Happy New Year!
Her dad told her:
Wishes come true more easily if we help them with effort every day.
And Sofía wrote her twelve wishes on a sheet of paper so she wouldn’t forget them. Something to think about: A wish comes true when we work a little for it every day.
